--- title: "What does reproducible mean?" subtitle: "Reproducible Workflows · Session 1" format: revealjs: footer: A. Stamm · Reproducible Workflows · Session 1 --- # Before the slides: what does "reproducible" mean to you? ## Class brainstorm {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **No slides, no spoilers: just you.** In pairs, spend **4 minutes** writing down everything you associate with the word *reproducible*. Don't filter, don't judge: - What does a *reproducible analysis* look like? - When is an analysis *not* reproducible? - Have you ever tried to **re-run** someone else's (or your own!) code months later? What happened? We'll collect your answers on the board, group them, and the session builds from there. :::
Going further

Pair-share (≈10 min total). 4 min in pairs, then we gather. There are no wrong answers: the point is to surface your prior experience, whatever your level.

## The reproducibility spectrum {.inv} Your answers cluster along a spectrum: where do your examples sit? ::: {.incremental .highlight-last} - **Scratch notes**: ideas in a notebook or a chat window; useful in the moment, impossible to re-run. - **Scripts**: code that *runs* and *re-runs*… on your machine, today. - **Reports**: prose *and* code together, with results woven into the narrative. - **Versioned analyses**: code under git, dependencies pinned, so it re-runs next year on another machine. - **Published analyses**: a report at a reachable URL that **anyone** can open and trust. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The aim of this course is to move every analysis you produce to the right-hand end: **an analysis that lives in a Quarto document, is versioned in git, has its dependencies pinned, and is published at a URL.** ::: # What is reproducibility? ## "Works here" vs "works anywhere" {.inv} The test is simple. Take an analysis you did last month and ask three questions: ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} **[Will it re-run?]{.green}**: does the code execute from source, with no hidden clicks or hand-fixes? **[Will it re-run *here*?]{.amber}**: does it reproduce on *your* machine tomorrow, when packages have updated? **[Will it re-run *anywhere*?]{.indigo}**: does it reproduce on a colleague's machine, or in a year? ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Everything in this course is in service of making each "will it re-run?" an unequivocal **yes**: for you, and for anyone else. ::: ## What breaks reproducibility {.inv} The enemies we'll learn to fight, one per later session: ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} **[The human memory gap]{.green}**: "I clicked through the wizard", "I cleaned it by hand in Excel". Code that lives nowhere but the analyst's head. **[The moving environment]{.amber}**: `install.packages()` happily updates *globally*, so your analysis breaks when a dependency version silently changes. **[The (dis)appearing data]{.indigo}**: reading a local file path only you have; data that can't be re-downloaded. **[The vanished machine]{.indigo}**: your laptop dies, your setup is gone. ::: ::: {.incremental .highlight-last} The *reproducibility habit* answers all four at once: **document your code, pin your environment, source your data, version everything.** ::: ## What reproducible research looks like {.inv} Here is the shape of every analysis we build this course: ::: {.incremental} 1. **Data** is **sourced** by code (a documented package, an open-data portal), never by manual download.2. The **analysis lives in a document** (Quarto) that mixes prose and code, so *seeing* the result shows *how* it was made. 3. **Dependencies are pinned** (`renv`/`uv`), so the document re-runs tomorrow. 4. **Everything is versioned** with git: every change, every step, reversible. 5. **It is published** to a URL others can reach. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} You already learned the R side: vectors, data frames, plotting. This course wraps that skill in a **workflow** so your results can be *trusted, shared and rebuilt by anyone, anywhere.* ::: ## The course at a glance {.inv} Over three sessions we climb from "it works on my machine" to "it's published and reproducible": ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} **[Session 1 · Write]{.green}**: your first Quarto documents: prose + code + results, transparent from source. **[Session 2 · Source]{.amber}**: source a real open-data set (any portal: data.gouv.fr or your own country's), *pin* it for reproducibility, and build the **portfolio book** it belongs to. **[Session 3 · Publish]{.indigo}**: version it with git, pin it with renv/uv, publish it to Posit Connect. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **By the end you'll have a published, versioned, reproducible portfolio**: and the habit of making every future analysis reproducible by default. ::: # Setting up your environment ## Your toolbox {.inv} One overarching language (R) plus a small publishing/versioning stack: ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} **[R]{.green}**: the language. Installed from CRAN. **[Positron]{.green}**: the IDE for both R *and* Python in this course. **[Quarto]{.amber}**: renders R *or* Python into documents, reports, slides and books: the heart of everything we do. **[uv (+ Python)]{.indigo}**: the fast Python setup/packaging tool we use to keep Python environments pinned, too. **[git + GitHub]{.indigo}**: version control; we add this in Session 3. ::: ## The Quarto wizard {.inv} The fastest way to get a Quarto project is the **Quarto wizard**, built right into Positron. ::: {.spread .spread-md} :::: .spread-cap Run *Quarto: Create Project* from the command palette, follow the prompts, and your first document appears and renders in seconds. :::: ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Live block (≈15 min).** Together: render the wizard's sample document, then open its source (`.qmd`) and its preview side by side. Change a heading, re-render, watch it update. ::: ## Verify your install {.inv} Run these and compare outputs: ```r R.version.string # e.g. "R version 4.6.1" ``` ::: mono quarto --version # in a terminal python3 --version git --version ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Rule of thumb.** If any of these errors, resolve it *now*: a broken toolchain will surface in every later session. The step-by-step guides are in `setup.qmd`. ::: # Quarto documents ## What is a Quarto document? {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} A **`.qmd`** file is plain text that mixes three things: **Markdown for prose**: headings, lists, emphasis, links, just like a README. **Code *cells*** that run R or Python when the document renders, with their output (numbers, figures, tables) written **into** the document. **YAML front matter** at the top (`title`, `format`, …) controlling how the whole thing is rendered. Render it once (`quarto render`, or *Preview* in Positron) and you get a **self-contained report**: the story *and* the evidence, generated from the same source. ::: ## Your first Quarto document {.inv} Minimal but complete: this *is* a reproducible analysis: ````markdown --- title: "My first report" format: html --- ```{{r}} x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10) mean(x) ``` ```` ::: {.callout-desc} **Inline code** runs R *inside a sentence* (backtick + `r` + expression); a **code cell** (fenced `{r}`) runs R and prints the result below it. Both re-evaluate on every render. ::: ## The YAML header {.inv} YAML is the control panel at the top of every document: ```yaml --- title: "My first report" author: "Your Name" format: html --- ``` ::: {.incremental} - `title`, `author`: metadata shown at the top of the page. - `format`: what to build, `html`, `pdf`, `docx`, `revealjs` (these slides are a `revealjs`), or a whole **book** (Session 2). - Any number of **additional options**: themes, table of contents, captions… ::: ::: {.callout-desc} YAML uses strict *key: value* pairs with two-space indentation. Indentation mistakes are the single most common Quarto error: read the error message, it usually points straight at the line. ::: ## Code cells: controlling what shows {.inv} By default a code cell shows **code + output**. You can show one, the other, or neither: ::: {.cell} ::: | Option | Effect | |---|---| | `echo: false` | hide the *code*, show the output | | `include: false` | show neither (setup code) | | `fig-cap: "..."` | caption a figure | | `message/warning: false` | silence package-load chatter | ::: {.callout-desc} Every option lives in a `#|` comment line just above the cell. Get into the habit of **captions for your figures** (`fig-cap`): they're what turn a pile of plots into a *report*. ::: ## `qmd` vs `rmd` {.inv} You may have heard of **R Markdown** (`.Rmd`), the older standard R uses. ::: {.incremental .highlight-last} - **`.qmd` (Quarto)** is the modern, language-agnostic successor. One tool that renders R *and* Python, with consistent options. - **`.rmd` (R Markdown)** still works, but we use **Quarto** for everything this term. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The same file can even mix R and Python cells: that's why your portfolio (Session 2) is Python-compatible by design. ::: ## A Quarto document in action {.inv} Everything so far is easier to *see* than to describe. Try it for yourself: - Open `common/portfolio-book/index.qmd` in Positron (or the wizard's sample document). - Press **Preview** (or Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+K) to render it. - Change a heading or a number, save, re-render, and the output updates to match the source. ::: {.callout-desc} The loop, **edit source → render → see output**, is the whole of Quarto. Everything else (figures, books, publishing) is that loop scaled up. ::: # Structured reporting & transparent code ## Literate programming {.inv} The idea at the heart of Quarto (**prose *and* code woven together**) has a name: ::: {.incremental} - **Literate programming** (Knuth, 1984): an analysis document is written primarily for *humans to read*, with the *code embedded* so the results it discusses appear in place. - The reader follows your *thinking*; the machine follows your *instructions*. - The document is **self-documenting**: the evidence sits beside the claim it supports. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Contrast with the *output-first* habit: a completed PDF with no source is only half an analysis. Here, the **source is the analysis**. ::: ## Structure a report for a reader {.inv} A reproducible report is a *document*, not a dump of output. Structure it: ::: {.incremental} 1. **Question first**: what are you asking, in one sentence? 2. **Data**: where it came from, how it was sourced (the code shows this). 3. **Cleaning decisions**: what you renamed, recoded, dropped, and *why*. 4. **Figures & tables**: each **captioned** and *referred to in the text*. 5. **Findings**: what you found, honestly, limits included. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **The caption habit.** A figure without a caption is a picture; a captioned figure *referred to in prose* is evidence. You'll practice this in Lab 2 and it becomes the backbone of your portfolio chapter. ::: ## Captions & cross-references {.inv} Quarto numbers and links your figures and tables automatically. This boxplot is a *live* captioned figure: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sepal length across iris species.](session-1_files/figure-revealjs/fig-iris-1.png){#fig-iris width=960} ::: ::: Now refer to it in prose with `@fig-iris`: > **Fig. @fig-iris** shows that setosa sepals are the shortest. Re-render this deck (or watch the number) and the cross-reference resolves automatically. ::: {.callout-desc} `@fig-…` / `@tbl-…` are **cross-references**: the number updates automatically if you move figures around. Every good report reads like a conversation with its own figures. ::: ## The transparency loop {.inv} Because source *is* the analysis, any reader can ask **"how did you make that?"** and get a real answer. ::: {.incremental} - This deck ships with a **code popover**: press `c` on any slide to see the source behind it. - That's the *habit* we want you to internalize for your own work: the analysis answers its own "how". - When someone asks "where does this number come from?", the answer is **"render the document"**, not "from my head". ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Lab 2 (≈30 min): build a structured report.** You'll write a short reproducible report on the penguins/iris data (with prose, a captioned figure, and a table), following the structure template below. ::: ## Your structured-report recipe {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} Here's a skeleton you'll reuse for every analysis this term. Copy it into `lab-2-structured-report.qmd` and fill it in: 1. **Title & author** in the YAML header. 2. **`## The question`**: one or two sentences. 3. **`## The data`**: code that reads or sources it. 4. **`## Cleaning`**: code + a short note of *what you decided and why*. 5. **`## Results`**: a captioned figure and a table, each **referred to in prose**. 6. **`## Findings`**: what you found, and what you did *not* find. :::
Going further

Resist the urge to make it long. A clean 5-section report beats 40 lines of unexplained code every time.

# Project preview: your portfolio book ## The end goal {.inv} Everything this course points toward is a single artefact: **your portfolio**. ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} **[A Quarto book]{.green}**: not slides, not a single report, but a *book* that grows all semester. **[Chapter 1 = your EDA]{.amber}**: a real dataset you care about, fetched by code from an open-data portal of your choice, analysed and cleaned. **[Versioned, pinned, published]{.indigo}**: under git, dependencies locked, reachable at a URL. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The scaffold already exists: `reproducible-workflows/common/portfolio-book/`. Copy it, render it, make it yours. We set up your actual **Chapter 1** in Session 2. ::: ## The semester plan {.inv} Here's how your book fills up over the term: ::: {.incremental} 1. **Session 1 (today)**: you learn the document mechanics; the book scaffold renders. 2. **Session 2**: you source a dataset by code (any open-data portal, data.gouv.fr or your own country's), clean it, and drop your EDA into **Chapter 1**. 3. **Session 3**: you put the book under **git**, pin it with **renv/uv**, and **publish** it. 4. **Later courses**: other instructors slot their work into the **placeholder chapters**, so the book keeps growing. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} By semester's end you hold a published, versioned, reproducible portfolio, and the skill to do it again for any analysis. ::: ## Three moves, one artefact {.dark auto-animate=true background-color="#17251F"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:88px; top:150px; width:720px; font-size:72px;"} Write, structure, grow. ::: ::: {.panel data-id="draft" style="left:840px; top:150px; width:150px; height:360px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="review" style="left:1006px; top:150px; width:150px; height:170px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="release" style="left:1006px; top:340px; width:150px; height:170px;"} ::: ## Write, structure, grow {.light auto-animate=true background-color="#F1EEE6"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:92px; top:104px; width:1100px; font-size:44px;"} Today you took the first reproducible steps. ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="draft" style="left:96px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Document]{.h} [Your analysis lives in a `.qmd`: YAML, code cells, inline `r`. Source *is* the report.]{.p} ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="review" style="left:470px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Structure & review]{.h} [Captions, cross-references, honest findings: a structured report (your lab-2) that a stranger can follow.]{.p} ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="release" style="left:844px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Grow the book]{.h} [The scaffold preview: a portfolio book that will keep filling all semester, chapter by chapter.]{.p} ::: ## Your Chapter 1 is next {.light auto-animate=true background-color="#F1EEE6"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:92px; top:104px; width:1100px; font-size:44px;"} From a rendering document to a book with content. ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="release" style="left:96px; top:200px; width:800px; height:400px;"} [Grow the book: Chapter 1 is next]{.h} [Every slide today built toward the same artefact: a book that grows. That chapter is step two toward the versioned, pinned, published portfolio you'll finish in Session 3.]{.p style="font-size:24px; line-height:1.6;"} ::: ::: {.panel .marker data-id="draft" style="left:944px; top:230px;"} ::: ::: {.panel .marker data-id="review" style="left:944px; top:290px;"} ::: ## Next time {.dark .finale auto-animate=true background-color="#17251F"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:200px; top:300px; width:880px; font-size:52px; text-align:center;"} Session 2: source your data, clean it, and build the book. ::: ::: {.panel data-id="draft" style="left:470px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="review" style="left:590px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="release" style="left:710px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {style="position:absolute; left:96px; top:600px; width:1024px; font-size:17px; color:rgba(241,238,230,0.62);"} Between sessions: make sure `quarto render` works on a trivial document (try the wizard), and skim [Quarto: Getting Started](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) for the parts we didn't cover. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
